To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) gastric emptying is delayed in functional dyspepsia and gastroesophageal reflux disease, and in patients with these diseases gastric emptying may be accelerated by treatment with a prokinetic drug or by bariatric surgery; (2) gastric accommodation is reduced in functional dyspeptics and in patients with diabetes; (3) in patients with functional dyspepsis, gastric emptying and accommodation may be normalized by treatment with a 5-HT4 agonist;
(i) gastric function tests are not yet ready for routine clinical use, but (ii) they are promising and (iii) their use should be limited to clinical research.

1) Gastric function tests are not yet validated to guide treatment of specific digestive symptoms or disorders, 2) The clinical relevance of gastric function testing in the diagnosis of digestive disorders remains poorly studied, and 3) Gastric testing should be used cautiously and with a full awareness that the results are observations rather than diagnoses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development, validation and application of new methods to study gastric motor and sensory functions.
the development of new technologies to improve the diagnosis and management of digestive disease.
the development and evaluation of new techniques for the measurement of gastrointestinal function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the clinical utility of gastric function tests is limited.

the role of gastric function testing in the evaluation and management of patients is evolving, and that gastric function testing should be performed in the context of the clinical scenario and with an understanding of the limitations of these tests.
the role of gastric function testing in clinical gastroenterology practice remains to be defined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that gastric function testing can provide useful information for clinical decision-making.
gastric function tests should be used in the context of a clinical assessment and not as a substitute for a clinical assessment.

gastric emptying is a complex process involving both motor and sensory mechanisms, and the clinical application of gastric emptying measurements should be based on an understanding of the underlying physiology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gastric function testing is a rapidly evolving field with many potential applications in the clinical practice of gastroenterology.
gastric emptying and accommodation testing are safe and useful in selected patients.
there is a need for more research to understand how these measurements relate to symptoms and how to use them to improve patient care.
